lines.text: Before electricity, when the sun went down, the world went dark. Really dark.
So what did people actually do all night? The answer is stranger than you think.
First, light cost money. Beeswax candles were for the rich. Most families burned smoky tallow, made from animal fat. The poorest just dipped dried rushes in grease.
In medieval towns, an evening bell told everyone to cover their fires, so wooden houses wouldn't burn down. Cover fire, in French, is couvre-feu. That's where we get the word curfew.
With no light and little to do, most people were in bed within an hour or two after dark.
But here's the twist. Historian Roger Ekirch found thousands of old records describing two sleeps. A first sleep, then waking up after midnight, and a second sleep until morning.
That break could last an hour or more, and people used it. They prayed, thought about their dreams, talked with family, tended the fire, and even visited the neighbors.
And yes, a few used the darkness to steal their neighbor's firewood.
Then came artificial light. Gas lamps, and later electric bulbs, kept the night bright. People stayed up later, and by the eighteen hundreds, that first sleep slowly stretched into one long night.
So if you ever wake up in the middle of the night, don't panic. For centuries, a break in the night was perfectly normal. Subscribe for more forgotten history.
